doc.title: Toshiko Akiyoshi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999

title: Why her music is difficult
summary: Her bebop foundation makes the music virtuosic; musicians like challenge.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: You know I never have written to make it difficult. But because my music, the foundation is bebop music, because that’s how I grew up. So bebop music, as you know, it’s a virtuoso music, it became virtuoso music after bebop. So consequently there are a lot of notes. And consequently it’s difficult. But I think a long time ago some classical musician said “the music has no difficulty but good and bad.” So sometimes music comes out difficult. Sometimes easy. But it doesn’t matter. Because most of the time I think in the classical field, they don’t really say that. And sometimes I think consider the challenge — if the pianist can play let’s say Rachmaninoff Concerto 3 or something like that and they consider it’s like a real technician, something like that, but they consider that challenging, they will not ever, ever — at least in my experience — say how come that was so hard. They don’t say that. But as for jazz somehow people say that. I heard a

long time ago somebody criticized my music, this was like over 15 years ago, said, “How come her music sounds so hard?” So Lew said, “Well hard yesterday, okay today, easy tomorrow.” So I think that’s why it tends to be difficult. But it’s two to tango you know. The musician, a good musician, I like to think they like challenging music. They will not — you know men, I shouldn’t say men — but a few of the artists, men and women both of them, live on bread alone. So I think challenging music is something that they would like — a challenge.
Well most of them, in L.A. a lot of the fellows and the women were working studio jobs and so forth, so they must have really relished this opportunity.
